newsitem.title: UK: WEEK AHEAD - Focus on UK rates, European data.
newsitem.headline: WEEK AHEAD - Focus on UK rates, European data.

text.p: British interest rates will provide a focus for financial markets in the week ahead as U.S. data slow to a trickle, analysts said on Friday.
U.S. markets were likely to cruise in neutral after the decision by the Federal Reserve to keep interest rates steady but dollar/yen could spark some interest.
In Britain, an announcement from the Bank of England monetary policy committee regarding interest rates is due on Thursday.
Many economists expect a rise from the current 6.5 percent, saying Labour's recent budget failed to take the economy off the boil.

"At the moment the market expectation is for a rise in interest rates of 50 basis points, although some people are starting to say they may only do 25 because of the effect that a 50 basis point rise might have on sterling," said Andrew Davies, bond analyst at London Bond Broking.
In a Reuters survey of 24 economists, 21 said they expected a rise in interest rates next week.
Analysts at Daiwa Europe in London also said sterling, which shot to a new six year high against the mark of 2.9620 on July 3, would be under the microscope.
"For sterling/mark we will watch to see if it reaches three marks to the pound," they said.
Ken Wattret, international economist at Paribas Capital Markets in London, said this was not out of the question.
"If we get a hike in rates that could give some more upward momentum to sterling," he said.
At 1244 GMT sterling was trading at 2.9582/92 marks.
But analysts said British bond markets were likely to react negatively to a rise in interest rates.
"Gilts have some problems to overcome if base rates are going to continue to go up," Wattret said.
Data in the U.S. will be slow in coming after the employment report reinforced the Fed's decision to keep interest rates on hold and sent U.S. markets shooting higher.
June U.S. payrolls rose 217,000 versus expectations of 222,000 and the jobless rate rose to five percent from 4.8 percent in May.

"The view has been firmly entrenched now that the Fed is on hold for some time," Wattret said. "It would probably take something pretty strong to change the prevailing bullish view and there is nothing in the calendar to turn the situation around."
Wattret said the producer price index on Friday would be the most important U.S. number in the week but that too was expected to be benign.
Forecasts were for June producer prices to be unchanged on the month, compared with a 0.3 percent fall in May, and for the core to rise 0.1 percent, versus a 0.3 percent fall previously.
Daiwa analysts also said the dollar/yen rate would be of interest as Japanese trade data for May arrive on Tuesday.
"The market will be looking to see if the yen moves against the dollar on the back of Japanese trade data," they said. The yen was currently trading at 113.43/3.53 to the dollar.
In continental Europe, analysts said markets' main concerns would be budgetary as countries strove to meet the budget deficit criteria to qualify for the European single currency.
Economic and finance ministers of the European Union meet on Monday. On the agenda is Italy's economic convergence plan for joining European Economic and Monetary Union (EMU).
Recently the 10-year BTP/Bund yield spread has squeezed in to a new record low at 101 basis points. Wattret said there was still scope for some further convergence.

"Although the fundamental outlook points to convergence having a bit further to run, I don't think we will see this speed of convergence continue. It'll be a much more consolidative phase from here," he said.
Also of interest was June German unemployment, due on Tuesday. Forecasts were for a seasonally adjusted increase of 20,000, compared with 50,000 in May.
"Unemployment is running at quite a high level and given the problems they are having in meeting the Maastricht criteria, any relaxation in that area would be welcome news," said Davies.
Wattret said that going by past experience there was likely to be some speculation about the numbers in the press on Monday.
"They are uncannily accurate so the market will react to them," he said.
